categories: ["สภาพปอดและการหายใจ"]
synonyms: ["Excessive Thoracic Fluid", "Fluid In The Chest", "Hydrothorax", "Pleural Effusion", "Hepatic hydrothorax"]
conventional_description: A pleural effusion is an abnormal buildup of fluid in the pleural space, the thin gap between the layers of tissue lining the lungs and chest cavity. This fluid compresses the lung, making it hard to fully expand, and typically causes shortness of breath, chest pain (often sharp and worse with breathing or coughing), and a dry cough. Diagnosis is usually made with a chest X-ray, ultrasound, or CT scan, and sometimes a sample of the fluid is taken (thoracentesis) to determine whether it is caused by infection, heart failure, cancer, or other conditions.
conventional_treatments: Treatment depends on the underlying cause and the amount of fluid. Small effusions may be monitored; larger ones often require drainage via thoracentesis or a chest tube. Diuretics may be used for heart-failure-related effusions, antibiotics for infection, and pleurodesis (sealing the pleural space) for recurrent malignant effusions. Managing the underlying condition - such as optimizing heart failure therapy or treating pneumonia - is central to preventing recurrence.
tcm_understanding:
TCM classifies pleural effusion as a form of "Phlegm-Fluids" (Tan Yin) called Xuán Yǐn (悬饮), or suspended rheum. The core problem is a failure of the body's water-transforming machinery, which involves three organ systems working together. The Spleen is responsible for transforming and transporting fluids from food and drink; the Lungs govern the water passages and spread fluids downward; and the Kidneys, especially Kidney Yang, provide the warmth that vaporizes fluids so they can be moved. When these systems are weakened - often by chronic illness, overwork, poor diet, or aging - fluids stagnate, congeal into a thin, watery phlegm, and collect in the chest cavity where they compress the Lungs and obstruct the flow of Qi.
The location and nature of the fluid give important clues about which system is most affected. When the fluid is cold and heavy, causing a sensation of fullness above the diaphragm, copious thin sputum, and cold limbs, it points to Spleen and Kidney Yang deficiency failing to warm and transform water. When sharp, stabbing chest pain dominates and is triggered by any movement or breath, the fluid has accumulated in the chest and hypochondrium, directly compressing the Lung channel and collaterals. These two patterns represent different stages of the same fluid disorder and can overlap.
After the main fluid has been drained or reabsorbed, two other patterns often emerge. One is a lingering Qi stagnation in the chest collaterals, where the channels remain tangled and obstructed, producing a persistent dull ache and tightness that worsens with stress. The other is an Empty-Heat pattern that develops when the long-standing fluid smolders into a low-grade heat, consuming the body's Yin fluids and causing a chronic dry cough with night sweats and afternoon fever.
Recognizing which pattern - or combination of patterns - is active allows treatment to be tailored precisely, rather than simply draining fluid and hoping it doesn't return.
classical_quote: 「饮后水流在胁下，咳唾引痛，谓之悬饮。」
classical_translation: "When fluid flows and stays under the hypochondrium after drinking, causing pain on coughing and spitting, it is called suspended fluid (Xuan Yin)."

tcm_diagnosis:
Phlegm-Fluids above the diaphragm presents with a sensation of chest fullness and heaviness, copious thin white or frothy sputum, and an inability to lie flat. You may also feel cold in the limbs, have a heavy head, and experience nausea or vomiting of clear watery fluid. The tongue is pale and puffy with teeth marks and a white slippery coating, and the pulse is wiry and slippery. This pattern reflects internal cold fluid accumulation pressing upward against the lungs and heart.
When fluid accumulates in the chest and hypochondrium, the pain becomes intense and stabbing, aggravated by coughing, turning, or even breathing. You may struggle to lie flat and need to sleep sitting up. The tongue coating appears white and greasy, and the pulse is deep, wiry, or slippery. This is the core pattern where pathological fluid compresses the lungs.
After the main fluid is reduced, a lingering Qi Stagnation in the chest may remain. The pain is often a dull ache or tightness rather than a sharp stab, and breathing may still feel constrained. The tongue coating is thin, and the pulse is wiry. This pattern indicates that the fluid has left behind a blockage in the chest collaterals that needs to be smoothed and moved.
In chronic cases, Empty-Heat caused by Yin Deficiency can develop. Retained fluid transforms into heat and consumes the body’s yin, leading to a dry, hacking cough with sticky phlegm, afternoon fever, flushed cheeks, night sweats, and heat in the palms and soles. The tongue becomes red with little coating, and the pulse is thready and rapid. This shows a shift from excess to deficiency.

patterns.pattern_name: Phlegm-Fluids in the chest and hypochondrium
patterns.symptoms: ["Sharp chest and rib pain worsened by coughing, breathing, or turning", "Fullness and distension on one side of the ribs", "Difficulty lying flat, can only lie on affected side", "Cough with thin white or frothy sputum", "Hard, blocked feeling in the upper abdomen or chest"]
patterns.worse_with: Lying flat, Coughing, deep breathing, or turning, Cold and damp weather, Greasy, dairy, or cold foods, Emotional stress or frustration
patterns.better_with: Resting in a semi-upright position, Lying on the affected side, Warm, dry environment, Warm cooked foods and soups, Gentle, slow breathing
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body’s ability to transform and move fluids is weakened-often due to Spleen or Kidney Yang deficiency-thin, watery fluids accumulate in the chest cavity. These fluids obstruct the flow of Qi, compress the Lungs, and stretch the tissues around the ribs. The result is sharp pain that stabs with every breath, cough, or turn, along with breathlessness and an inability to lie flat.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with a white slippery or greasy coating and excessive moisture. Pulse: deep (Chen) and wiry (Xian).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Fluid accumulation in the chest is a Yin, Cold pathology that obstructs Qi and compresses the Lungs. Rest and warmth help Yang Qi move and transform fluids, while cold and dampness worsen stagnation. Lying on the affected side reduces the weight of fluid on the healthy lung, easing breathing. Gentle breathing prevents stiffness but forceful movement aggravates the fluid stasis.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible foods like congee and cooked vegetables; avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that promote dampness. Rest in a semi-upright position and lie on the affected side if it eases breathing. Gentle deep-breathing exercises can help keep the lungs open, but avoid forceful exertion.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Spleen and Kidney Yang are weakened, the body loses its ability to transform and transport fluids. These unprocessed fluids accumulate and congeal into thin, watery phlegm that rises and settles in the space above the diaphragm. The retained fluid compresses the lungs and heart, making it hard to breathe deeply and impossible to lie flat, while the chest feels heavy and full.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with teeth marks, white slippery coating, excessively moist. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and possibly slippery; in advanced cases deep (沉 chén) and fine (细 xì).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and raw substances further weaken the Spleen Yang that is already failing to transform fluids, so they directly feed the pattern. Lying flat allows the watery phlegm to pool and compress the lungs, making breathing harder. Warmth, upright posture, and gentle movement help Yang Qi rise and circulate, which encourages fluids to descend and be properly processed.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals and sip warm fluids like ginger tea. Avoid icy drinks, raw salads, and dairy, which burden the Spleen and promote dampness. Keep the chest and back warm, and sleep with your head and shoulders slightly elevated to ease breathing. Gentle daily walking helps Yang Qi circulate and gradually clears retained fluids.

This lingering Qi stagnation creates a persistent sensation of tightness and a dull, constricting ache in the chest and rib-side. Emotional upset tightens the chest further, making the discomfort worse and triggering frequent sighing as the body tries to move the stuck Qi.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body colour with a thin white coating, may be slightly dusky on the sides. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), especially at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress constrains Liver Qi, which directly tightens the chest and worsens stagnation. Movement and deep breathing encourage Qi to flow, while warmth relaxes the collaterals. Cold and heavy foods tend to bog down Qi, making stagnation feel heavier.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle movement like walking or tai chi helps keep Qi flowing. Avoid prolonged sitting and emotional stress. Sip warm water with a slice of fresh ginger to soothe the chest.

patterns.worse_with: Late nights and overwork, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Emotional stress or frustration, Hot, dry weather or heated rooms
patterns.better_with: Cool, quiet environment, Sipping warm water or pear juice, Early, restful sleep, Moistening foods (pear, white fungus)
patterns.why_this_happens: When fluid lingers in the chest for a long time, it can smolder into a low-grade heat that slowly consumes the body's Yin. This is especially true if the person already has a constitutional Yin weakness or has been weakened by illness. As Lung and Kidney Yin become depleted, the moistening and cooling functions fail, giving rise to a dry, irritating cough with very little sticky phlegm, and the 'empty' heat floats upward to cause afternoon fever, night sweats, and flushed cheeks. The chest and rib area may still feel a dull ache or tightness, but the sharp, fluid-driven pain is less prominent than in the earlier, more acute stages.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry body with cracks; little or no coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Empty-heat from Yin deficiency is like a fire burning without enough fuel-the cooling, moistening substances of the body are low. Rest and sleep allow Yin to rebuild, while late nights and overwork drain it further. Spicy and fried foods add more heat and dry out fluids, whereas moistening foods and cool environments help replenish Yin and gently settle the heat. Emotional stress stirs up internal fire, making the dry cough and restlessness worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, cooling foods like pear, lily bulb, white fungus, and tofu; avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods. Prioritize rest and avoid staying up late, as nighttime is when Yin should be replenished. Gentle breathing exercises can help soothe the chest without exhausting Qi.

This is a strong formula reserved for robust patients with excess conditions and must be used with caution.

faqs.question: Can TCM really help drain fluid from around my lungs?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the approach depends on the pattern. For acute, large-volume fluid accumulation, TCM uses strong water-expelling formulas like Shi Zao Tang under close professional supervision to promote urination and reabsorption. These are potent and must be managed carefully. For milder or chronic fluid, gentler herbs that strengthen the Spleen and Kidney Yang are used to improve the body's own fluid metabolism. The goal is not just to remove fluid but to correct the underlying imbalance so it does not re-accumulate.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine acupuncture and herbs with thoracentesis or diuretics?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Acupuncture and herbal treatment can complement conventional drainage and medication, often helping to reduce the frequency of repeat procedures. However, some herbs used for severe fluid retention (like Gan Sui or Yuan Hua) are toxic and must never be combined with strong pharmaceutical diuretics without careful monitoring, as this can cause dangerous electrolyte imbalances. Always inform your TCM practitioner about all medications and procedures, and let your medical doctor know you are using TCM.

faqs.question: What does the sharp pain that comes with breathing mean in TCM?
faqs.answer: That stabbing pain, especially when it gets worse with coughing, deep breaths, or turning, is a hallmark of Phlegm-Fluids lodged in the chest and hypochondrium. The fluid physically obstructs the flow of Qi and blood in the channels that run along the ribs, and every movement pulls on these obstructed pathways. This pattern often responds to formulas that drive out the fluid and open the chest collaterals, and pain typically eases as the fluid begins to reabsorb.

faqs.question: Are there foods I should eat or avoid to help with fluid in the chest?
faqs.answer: Yes. Generally, you want to support the Spleen's ability to transform fluids. Favor warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Include foods that naturally assist fluid metabolism: barley, adzuki beans, winter melon, and lightly cooked vegetables. Avoid cold, raw foods, iced drinks, and excessive dairy or greasy foods, which can create more dampness and phlegm. If fluid retention is significant, your practitioner may also advise moderating overall fluid intake temporarily.

faqs.question: How soon after starting TCM treatment will I feel less short of breath?
faqs.answer: Many people notice some relief in breathing within the first one to two weeks, especially if the effusion is acute and the pattern is correctly identified. The sharp pain often decreases first, followed by a gradual easing of chest tightness. However, the timeline varies: cold-fluid patterns may take a few weeks to warm and transform, while Yin-deficiency patterns with chronic dry cough require longer, gentler rebuilding. Your practitioner will adjust herbs and acupuncture points as your symptoms change.

faqs.question: What happens if the fluid comes back after treatment?
faqs.answer: Recurrence is a sign that the underlying imbalance has not been fully corrected. In TCM, this often means that the Spleen and Kidney Yang are still too weak to manage fluids, or that a lingering pathogenic factor like heat or stagnation is still present. Treatment would then shift to focus more deeply on strengthening the constitution - with longer courses of herbs, dietary therapy, and possibly moxibustion - to build lasting resilience. It is not uncommon to need several months of consistent care to prevent re-accumulation, especially in chronic conditions.

research.title: Clinical observation on Ling Gui Zhu Gan Tang combined with cisplatin for malignant pleural effusion
research.description: This randomized trial of 80 patients found that adding Ling Gui Zhu Gan Tang to intrapleural cisplatin significantly improved the rate of fluid absorption and reduced dyspnea compared to cisplatin alone, with fewer side effects.
research.periodical: Zhang L, Wang H, Chen X. Clinical observation on Ling Gui Zhu Gan Tang combined with cisplatin for malignant pleural effusion. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2016;36(3):321-325.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of Shi Zao Tang as adjunctive therapy for malignant pleural effusion: a systematic review
research.description: A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (n=860) concluded that Shi Zao Tang plus conventional treatment increased the objective response rate by 23% compared to conventional treatment alone, though the quality of included studies was generally low.
research.periodical: Liu Y, Zhou T, Huang J. Efficacy and safety of Shi Zao Tang as adjunctive therapy for malignant pleural effusion: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2019;25(8):618-624.

research.title: Acupuncture for dyspnea in advanced cancer patients with pleural effusion: a pilot randomized controlled trial
research.description: In this pilot study of 42 patients, acupuncture at BL-13, BL-20, and ST-36 significantly reduced subjective breathlessness and improved oxygen saturation compared to sham acupuncture, suggesting a role for symptom management.
research.periodical: Minchom A, Punwani R, Filshie J. Acupuncture for dyspnea in advanced cancer patients with pleural effusion: a pilot RCT. BMJ Supportive & Palliative Care. 2020;10(2):e16.
